title: What each text asked
hookLine: each text asked something different of its readers
tomorrow: so could you staple all these books into one big scripture?

lines: THE WHOLE TORAH ON ONE FOOT.
cards: Someone asks for the short version of a thing that took you years. Give me the summary. One line.
The Talmud tells of a man who brought that request to two teachers, one of them Hillel, the sage of Pirkei Avot from a few weeks back, as a dare: teach me the whole Torah while I stand on one foot.
Shammai pushes him away with the builder's measuring rod in his hand. Hillel takes the dare.

teach.h: WHAT IS HATEFUL TO YOU, DON'T DO.
teach.b: What is hateful to you, Hillel says, don't do to your neighbor. That is the whole Torah.

teach.h: THE REST IS COMMENTARY. GO AND LEARN.
teach.b: The rest is commentary. Then the odd part: go and learn. Here's the puzzle.
If one line is the whole Torah, why send the man off to study? Because in Jewish teaching both are true.

The line is real, and it's a door, not the house. Study itself is counted among the commandments; an old teaching in the Mishnah says it equals all the rest together. The commentary is how the line gets lived.

teach.h: ASK EACH BOOK FOR ITS LINE.
teach.b: Now turn to this shelf and ask each book for its one-foot line. You won't get one answer. The Dhammapada: avoid evil, do good, purify your mind.
The Analects: learn, and practice what you learn. The Quran's short surah on time: believe, do good, urge one another to truth and patience. Ecclesiastes: remember now, and eat your bread with joy.
Each asks its own, in its own words, of its own people. One to tell a friend tonight: Hillel's well-known one-line answer doesn't end at the summary. It ends with an order: go and learn.
The puzzle, solved: a summary is where learning starts, and each text's starting line is different.

how: Hillel's answer is retold in Jewish teaching as a model of patience and of study: the summary, then 'go and learn'. Readers of several traditions keep a short line from a text as a doorway into the rest of it.

games.q: what does “what each text asked” mean?
o: the questions readers ask about a hard text
the particular thing each sacred text asks of you
the one rule every scripture secretly agrees on

games.q: ask each text for its one line: tap the pairs.
p: what is hateful to you, don't do
avoid evil, do good, purify the mind
learn, and practice what you learn

s: Hillel's one-foot answer ends with the summary
he adds: the rest is commentary; go and learn.
in the story, Shammai sends the man away
he pushes him off with the builder's measuring rod in his hand.
every book on this shelf asks the same thing underneath
the Dhammapada, the Analects, the Quran and Ecclesiastes each ask something of their own.

games.q: a friend says, 'give me the one-line version of the Gita and i'll skip the rest.' what does Hillel's story point to?
o: the one line is real, and it's a door: now go and learn the rest.
one line is enough; everything after it is just extra detail.
refuse to sum it up at all, the way Shammai did.
games.why: Hillel did sum it up, then sent the man to study: 'the rest is commentary; go and learn.'

practice: Take a pen and a scrap of paper and write three short lines, one ask from each of three texts you met on this shelf, in your own words. Read them back slowly.
Notice where they ask different things of you, and leave the differences alone.

wordCard.voice: What each text asked: the one-foot line each book gives, and the learning that goes on past it.

orig.note: Aramaic, from the Talmud: go and learn, Hillel's last words to the man on one foot.

carryVoice: Pocket this one: each asks its own, and a one-line summary is a door, not the house. Talk tomorrow.

sources.ref: Babylonian Talmud, Shabbat 31a (the man on one foot; Shammai's measuring rod; Hillel: what is hateful to you, do not do to your fellow; the rest is commentary; go and learn)
Mishnah Peah 1:1 (the study of Torah is set against all the other commandments)
Dhammapada 183 (not to commit sin, to do good, to purify one's mind)
Analects 1.1; Quran 103; Ecclesiastes 12:1 and 9:7 (the one-line asks named in the teach)
